 Was Mauricio Pochettino’s time with the USMNT a success?
 By
 Andy Edwards , 
 By
 Andy Edwards 
     Published November 17, 2026 12:39 PM 
 Add 
 on Google 
 Facebook 
 Twitter 
 Email
 Add 
 on Google 
 USMNT boss Mauricio Pochettino is set to become the new Manchester United manager later this week, closing the book on the Argentine’s 26-month foray into American soccer.
 MORE — What/who next for USMNT? | USA 6-0 Haiti | Poch’s tough task at Man United 
 They won more than they lost (22W-2D-12L), and the USMNT, generally speaking, is in a better place now than it was before Pochettino took over. U.S. Soccer’s next hire will be a gargantuan task to get right, due in large part to the fact that Pochettino had hit most of the pertinent metrics and there was genuine excitement over the direction that the program was moving.
 Reaching round of 16 at 2026 World Cup: B-
 The remit for Pochettino’s initial contract (signed in September 2024) was to lead the USMNT at the 2026 World Cup on home soil. His appointment came not only as a significant shock, but during a period of incredible turbulence and upheaval. Gregg Berhalter had just been fired after failing to get out of the group stage at Copa America 2024 (finishing behind Uruguay and Panama, neither of whom achieved the same feat two years later) and the first half of the most important World Cup cycle in American history had, effectively, been wasted. 
 To put it bluntly, the USMNT job was not an attractive one at the time. Star players under-performing had become the norm, there wasn’t another truly competitive game to speak of for two more years, and a serious disconnect between the fanbase and the team/federation made it downright unenjoyable to follow the Yanks. They didn’t just need a top coach, they needed a unifier and a figurehead who could set everything straight and save us all from the most disastrous World Cup of our lifetimes. 
 It’s easy to forget all of that context these days, when the only thing that matters is what have you done for me lately . Heck, it’s apparently also easy to forget how well the USMNT played in their first two games of that World Cup, against two teams that also advanced, and the fact they won their first knockout game in 24 years a couple of weeks later. Pochettino made USMNT fans, American soccer fans and soccer-adjacent sports fans alike feel excited and hopeful about a sport they’d either been devoted to for their entire lives or just watched their very first game, and for a few days, he had them thinking, “Why not us?” Prior to the situation surrounding Folarin Balogun’s red card, the USMNT was a World Cup darling and a feel-good story at the world’s biggest and greatest sporting event.
 Longtime USMNT fans — the ones who woke up at 3 am to watch them play in 2002 — know how far we’ve come and won’t forget the summer of 2026 for as long as we live, no matter how many goals Belgium beat them by.
 Creating competitive, demanding culture: A-
 The players (especially the stars) had too much power and they saw USMNT camps as something of a relaxed recreational period before Pochettino took over, so the first thing he did was bring them back down to Earth and make it clear that everybody — and he meant everybody — was there to compete for their job every training session and every game. This led to some players being left off of the roster for a time and others disappearing from the USMNT conscience altogether, but by the time the World Cup rolled around most of them had accepted that it was Pochettino’s way or the highway.
 The one possible exception who might not be so sorry to see Pochettino leave is Christian Pulisic, who famously skipped the 2025 CONCACAF Gold Cup, the key competitive tournament that would afford Pochettino the best chance to assess his team a year out from the World Cup (they lost the final to Mexico). The two of them traded some words in the public realm last summer and the working relationship seemed to be solid enough upon Pulisic’s return to the team, but he remains one of only a few players out of whom Pochettino didn’t get their best. That, plus good health, may have made more of a difference against Belgium (and earned Pochettino A+ across the board).
 Implementing real “change” in American soccer: Incomplete
 Define “change” however you like — there’s only so much that the head coach of the senior national team can affect — but that’s what the next four years of Pochettino’s tenure were supposed to be about. 
 This was the part that should have excited USMNT fans most: Pochettino is a team builder much more so than he is a game manager, and just one camp into his first full World Cup cycle he had already begun to do what he does best. Pochettino guiding and developing teenagers Cavan Sullivan, Julian Hall, Mathis Albert, Neil Pierre and Adri Mehmeti — even from afar as their national team coach — was the best possible future for the USMNT, and undoubtedly a key factor when the powers that be at U.S. Soccer re-signed him after the World Cup. Of course his name would come up anytime a top European job came open — he knew it and they knew it — but that’s a risk you take competing at the highest level of the sport.
 Pochettino’s football was a nearly perfect stylistic and tactical fit for the USMNT and its player pool. U.S. Soccer shouldn’t stray too far from that path with their next hire.
